client: I've been really struggling since my dad passed away two months ago — it was so sudden, and I just wasn't prepared for it at all. Everything feels kind of gray and hollow now, like I go through the motions of my day but nothing actually feels meaningful anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I guess I'm here because I didn't know what else to do.
therapist:
I'm really glad you're here, even if it doesn't feel like it will help yet — reaching out when everything feels gray and hollow takes a quiet kind of courage. Losing your dad so suddenly, without any chance to prepare, is a profound loss, and that sense of just going through the motions makes complete sense right now. I want you to know there's no pressure to "fix" anything today — I'm just here to walk alongside you. 

Can you tell me a little more about what a typical day looks like for you right now, and maybe when that hollow feeling tends to hit hardest?

client: Honestly, most days I just kind of drift through. I wake up, make coffee, stare at my phone for a while, maybe go to work if I can pull myself together enough. The hollow feeling is worst in the evenings, I think, because that's when I used to call him.
therapist: Those evening hours sound especially painful — that specific time when you'd normally hear his voice is now a kind of daily reminder of the absence, and that's a very particular kind of grief. It makes a lot of sense that the rest of the day feels like drifting when you're quietly bracing for that hard moment each night. I'm curious — when you find yourself staring at your phone or going through those motions, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind, even quietly in the background?

client: Honestly, the thoughts that run through my head are kind of embarrassing to say out loud. It's mostly like... wondering if he's doing fine without me, if he even notices the silence on his end, and then this creeping feeling that maybe I was just easier to leave behind than I thought. And underneath all of that there's this quiet voice asking if I'm ever going to stop waiting for something that's not coming back.
therapist: Thank you for trusting me with that — those thoughts aren't embarrassing at all, they're actually really human and tender, and it takes courage to say them out loud. That quiet voice wondering if you were "easier to leave behind" stands out to me gently — it sounds like part of you is turning his death into a story about your own worth, which is such a common but painful thing grief can do to us. I want to explore that with you a little — when you hear that thought that you were easy to leave behind, what feels true about it to you, and where do you think it comes from?

client: I think it comes from... a lot of places, honestly. Like, we weren't that close near the end — he had his own life, his own friends, and I always felt like I was on the edges of it, never quite in the center. So when he died and I realized how much time had passed since we'd really talked, it just kind of confirmed something I'd already been afraid was true about myself — that I'm the kind of person people can drift away from without really noticing.
therapist: What you just shared is really significant — it sounds like his death didn't just bring grief, it felt like it confirmed a fear you've been carrying quietly for a long time, maybe long before he passed. I want to gently pause on something though: the fact that *you* kept calling him, that *you* noticed the distance and felt it so deeply, actually tells a different story about who you are than "someone people don't notice." Can you think of any other relationships in your life — past or present — where the evidence might push back against this idea that you're someone who gets left behind without being missed?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I want to believe it, but my mind immediately goes to all the ways it doesn't hold up. Like, yeah, I kept calling him, but maybe that just means I was the one who needed more, not that I was genuinely valued. It's hard to think of examples that push back against it because whenever someone does seem to care, I find myself wondering if it's real or if they just haven't gotten tired of me yet.
therapist: That pattern you just described — where care from others gets filtered out or explained away, but evidence of being overlooked gets absorbed as truth — is actually a really important thing to notice, and it's at the heart of what keeps this painful belief alive. Your mind has become very skilled at protecting that core fear by discounting anything that contradicts it, which isn't a character flaw, it's just a story that got written a long time ago and has been defending itself ever since. I'm wondering — when do you think you first started believing that you were someone people could drift away from without noticing, because I have a feeling this didn't start with your dad?

client: I sat with that for a second because it actually hit kind of hard. I think... maybe middle school? There was this group of friends I had, and one day I just sort of noticed they'd made plans without me, and when I asked about it nobody really had an explanation, they just kind of shrugged. It didn't feel like a big dramatic falling out, it was more like I just quietly stopped mattering, and I remember thinking that must mean something about me specifically.
therapist: That moment sounds quietly devastating in a way that's almost harder than a big dramatic falling out — there was no explanation, no closure, just a shrug, and your young mind had to make sense of it somehow, and the story it landed on was "this must mean something is wrong with me." It makes so much sense that a version of you has been carrying that conclusion ever since, looking for proof of it in every relationship including with your dad. I'm gently curious — if a child you cared about told you that story, that they were left out and nobody explained why, would *you* conclude that it meant something was fundamentally wrong with them?

client: I mean... no, obviously not. If a kid told me that, I'd probably think the other kids were just being thoughtless, or maybe there was some stupid social drama that had nothing to do with them. But it's different when it's me — like, I know that's what I'm supposed to say, that it wasn't my fault, but it doesn't actually feel true when I'm the one sitting with it.
therapist: You just did something really important there — you could see clearly that a child in that situation wouldn't deserve that conclusion, but when it comes to yourself, the knowing and the *feeling* are living in completely different places. That gap between what we intellectually understand and what we emotionally believe is exactly where a lot of this work lives, and just noticing it honestly like you did is genuinely meaningful progress. I'm wondering — what do you think it would take, even just a small step, for that compassionate explanation you'd offer a child to start feeling even a little bit true when you turn it toward yourself?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but honestly it feels like there's this wall I can't get past. Like, I can say the kind words out loud, I can even mean them in some abstract way, but the moment I turn them toward myself it's like my brain just rejects them, like they don't apply to me specifically. I don't know what it would take to make that gap smaller, and I guess I'm a little scared that maybe for me it just... stays that way.
therapist: That fear — that maybe the wall is just permanent for you specifically — is worth taking seriously rather than dismissing, because it's clearly real and it's been there a long time. But I want to gently offer this: the fact that your brain rejects these kind words *specifically when aimed at yourself* isn't evidence that you're a hopeless case, it's actually evidence of how deeply that old story got wired in — and what gets learned, even very early and very thoroughly, can shift with time and the right kind of practice. We don't have to knock the wall down all at once — I'm curious, is there even one small moment you can recall, however brief, where you felt genuinely okay about yourself, even if it didn't last long?

client: I have to think really hard about that... there was maybe one moment, a few years ago, when I finished a project at work that I'd been struggling with for months, and for like half a day I actually felt like maybe I wasn't completely useless. But even saying that out loud, I'm already second-guessing it — like, was I actually feeling good about myself, or was I just relieved it was over? It's hard to tell the difference, and I'm not sure that counts as what you're asking for.
therapist: The fact that you had to think hard to find it, and then immediately questioned whether it even counts, actually tells me something important — that moment is real, and your mind's instinct to shrink it or explain it away is the same pattern we've been talking about all along. Whether it was pride or relief, something in you recognized that *you* had done something hard, and for half a day that felt true — that's not nothing, that's actually a small crack in the wall. I'm curious, what do you think it would look like to treat that memory with the same generosity you'd offer someone else — to let it count, just for now, without needing to qualify it?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to just accept it, but there's this immediate voice that says "you're being self-indulgent if you make too big a deal out of one half-day." It's like even trying to be generous with myself feels like I'm setting myself up to be proven wrong later, like I'll just disappoint myself again. I don't know how to let something count without it feeling fragile or risky.
therapist: That voice calling self-compassion "self-indulgent" is such a telling one — it's essentially saying you need to stay small and guarded to stay safe, which makes sense as a protection strategy, but it also means you never get to actually rest inside a good moment. And that fear of letting something count because it might make the eventual disappointment worse — that's not weakness, that's someone who has been hurt enough times that hope itself started to feel dangerous. I'm wondering, what do you think that protective voice is trying to keep you safe from, and has staying guarded actually made the painful moments hurt less, or has it just meant you faced them more alone?
